questions.question: What basic items should I put in a wildfire grab-and-go bag?

response.answer: A basic grab-and-go bag includes bottled water, ready-to-eat food like high-calorie power bars, a phone charger, a battery bank, a radio, a flashlight, and extra batteries. It also contains seasonal clothing, an emergency blanket, a whistle, a pen and notepad, a small first aid kit, and personal medications. Basic items include toiletries such as an extra pair of glasses or contact lenses and solution, as well as a copy of your emergency plan and important documents like insurance papers.

questions.question: What are some practical FireSmart actions I can take around my home?

response.answer: Complete a self-assessment of your property with the FireSmart Home Assessment tool, clean gutters and roofs, and keep decks and balconies clear of leaves and debris. Keep grass and weeds cut below 10 centimetres, move firewood and lumber 10-30 meters away from your property, and relocate propane tanks 10-30 meters away with 10 meters of combustible vegetation clearance. Prune trees to create a two-meter clearance from the ground to the lowest branches, hold sheds and other structures to the same standards, and reduce flammable plants using the landscaping guide. Select low-density, fire-resistant plants and shrubs, avoid woody debris and mulch near the home, and maintain a 1.5-metre non-combustible zone around your entire home and attachments. Remember to cut grass along fence lines because long, dry grass easily ignites, and give sheds and outbuildings the same FireSmart considerations.

questions.question: How can my household stay connected during a wildfire emergency?

response.answer: Make an emergency plan to establish how you will communicate and connect with loved ones if you become separated, and keep copies in your grab-and-go bags. Keep your phone fully charged and preserve battery life by dimming your screen and avoiding power-hungry apps and videos. Create family and emergency contact lists and program them into your phone for quick access. Use texts, emails, and social media because data-based services are less likely to experience major interruptions during disasters. Consider setting up a virtual meeting place, such as a closed Facebook group, for family to check in during an emergency.

questions.question: What general steps can reduce my exposure to wildfire smoke?

response.answer: Managing indoor air quality at home is the best way to reduce your smoke exposure. Stay inside as much as possible by keeping windows and doors closed, closing fresh air intakes, and setting air conditioning to recirculate. Use a portable HEPA air cleaner or do-it-yourself air cleaner, turn on high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, and consider using a humidifier. Visit public spaces such as community centres, libraries, and shopping malls that have cleaner, cooler indoor air. Limit outdoor exercise and physical activity on smoky days, stopping or reducing activity if breathing becomes difficult or uncomfortable. Drink plenty of fluids or water to help reduce inflammation. Consider wearing a well-fitted N95/KN95/KF94 respirator if you need to be outdoors. Keep your cleaner air space comfortably cool using air conditioners, heat pumps, evaporative coolers, fans, and window shades.

questions.question: Should I activate my structure-protection sprinklers while evacuating?

response.answer: If you have installed a structure protection sprinkler system on your property DO NOT activate your system as you are evacuating. Structure Protection Specialists will activate sprinkler systems when the time is right. Pre-emptively activating structure protection sprinkler systems can drain reservoirs and deplete valuable water resources that first responders depend on to protect homes, neighbourhoods and communities.

questions.question: How should I prepare both my emergency plan and my grab-and-go bags?

response.answer: To prepare your emergency plan, start by downloading a fill-in-the-blanks emergency plan from www.gov.bc.ca/PreparedBC to compile vital information and establish how you will communicate and connect if separated. When you are done, make copies of your emergency plan for grab-and-go bags at home, at work, and in your vehicle. Build grab-and-go bags for each member of your household, starting with a basic list and customizing them for additional household needs such as pets, young children, seniors, or people with disabilities. A basic bag list includes bottled water and ready-to-eat food, a phone charger and battery bank, a small radio and flashlight (battery-powered or hand-crank), extra batteries, a whistle, a pen and notepad, a small first aid kit and personal medications, toiletries including extra glasses or contact lenses, seasonal clothing and an emergency blanket, and a copy of your emergency plan and important documents such as insurance papers.

questions.question: Which household and yard changes should I prioritize to reduce wildfire risk?

response.answer: Changes made to the area closest to your home, and your home itself, have the greatest impact in reducing your risk of wildland fire damage. Maintain a 1.5 metre non-combustible surface around your home and any attachments, like decks. Keep grass and weeds cut below 10 centimetres. Avoid planting flammable trees and plants, such as cedar, spruce, juniper, pine and tall grasses. Do not use bark or pine needle mulches within 10 metres of your home, as they are highly combustible; gravel mulch and decorative crushed rock mulch significantly reduce the risk of wildland fire. Firewood piles should be stored at least 10 metres from your home. Clean and maintain gutters and roofs, and keep decks and balconies clear of leaves and debris. Prune trees to create a two-meter clearance from the ground to the lowest branches.

questions.question: How should I change my activity and indoor environment during wildfire smoke?

response.answer: Take it easy and limit outdoor exercise on smoky days because the harder you breathe, the more smoke you inhale. If your breathing becomes difficult or uncomfortable, stop or reduce the activity, stay cool, and drink plenty of fluids. Drink lots of water to help reduce inflammation. Stay inside as much as possible, keep windows and doors closed, close fresh air intakes, set air conditioning to recirculate, and turn on HEPA filters. Use a portable HEPA air cleaner or a do-it-yourself air cleaner to filter the air in your home. Visit public spaces such as community centres, libraries, and shopping malls which tend to have cleaner, cooler indoor air.

FireSmart Begins at Home Guide
Completing all FireSmart recommendations will greatly increase a structure’s survivability

PROTECT YOUR HOME
British Columbians play a critical role in mitigating wildfire risks around
their homes and properties by undertaking FireSmartTM activities.
Simple measures, such as focussing on FireSmart’s three priority zones,
can make a significant difference to the survivability of structures by
decreasing the intensity of a wildfire and slowing its spread.

● FireSmart BC is a provincial program committed to reducing the negative impacts of
wildfire.
● FireSmart BC is the go-to resource for individuals, neighbourhoods and communities
looking to protect themselves and their properties from wildfire.
● FireSmart BC is based on scientific research that shows that doing simple FireSmart
tasks around where you live can make your property more resilient to wildfire.

questions.question: I installed structure-protection sprinklers, so I should turn them on as I evacuate, right?

response.answer: If you have installed a structure protection sprinkler system on your property DO NOT activate your system as you are evacuating. Structure Protection Specialists will activate sprinkler systems when the time is right. Pre-emptively activating structure protection sprinkler systems can drain reservoirs and deplete valuable water resources that first responders depend on to protect homes, neighbourhoods and communities.
